prompt: Naive string matching for text length n and pattern length m — which two statements are correct?
options: The runtime is O((n−m+1)·m), because every shift is tested independently.
No information gained at one shift is carried over to the next one.
The runtime is O(n+m), because each character is read only once.
Naive matching finds a different set of valid shifts than Rabin-Karp does.
explanation: n−m+1 shifts × up to m comparisons ✓, and the absence of any carry-over is exactly the weakness the smarter algorithms fix ✓. O(n+m) is Rabin-Karp's *expected* bound ✗, and all three algorithms return exactly the same set of valid shifts ✗.

prompt: What is the core idea of the Rabin-Karp algorithm?
options: Compare a numeric fingerprint (hash) of each text window against the pattern's fingerprint instead of comparing characters.
Precompute a finite automaton that reads the text in a single pass.
Sort text and pattern, then binary-search.
Build a suffix tree of the text.
explanation: Treating P and every length-m window of T as base-d numbers reduces an O(m) character comparison to an O(1) numeric one. The rolling update computes the next window's value from the current one in O(1). Option 2 describes FSM matching, the other two are unrelated.

prompt: Rabin-Karp's rolling hash — which two statements are correct?
options: t_{sft+1} = 10·(t_sft − 10^{m−1}·T[sft]) + T[sft+m] computes the next window's value in O(1).
The pattern value p and the first window value t₀ are computed in Θ(m) using Horner's rule.
The rolling update costs Θ(m), since the whole window has to be re-read.
The constant 10^{m−1} must be recomputed for every shift.
explanation: Subtract the leading digit's contribution, shift up, add the new trailing digit — O(1) ✓ — and Horner's rule gives the two initial values in Θ(m) ✓. That O(1) update is the entire point, so options 3 and 4 defeat it ✗✗ (10^{m−1} is precomputed once).

prompt: In Rabin-Karp with modulus q, the test t_sft ≡ p (mod q) succeeds. What follows?
options: sft *may* be a valid shift — a spurious hit is possible, so an explicit character check is required.
sft is definitely a valid shift; no further check is needed.
sft is definitely not a valid shift.
The algorithm has failed and must restart with a different q.
explanation: Working modulo q makes the test sound but imprecise: t_sft ≢ p proves a non-match (no false negatives), while t_sft ≡ p may be a spurious hit ("unechter Treffer"). Every hash hit therefore needs a character-by-character verification.

prompt: Why is Rabin-Karp computed modulo a prime q at all? Which two statements are correct?
options: Without the modulus, p and t_sft can exceed a machine word for long patterns, breaking the O(1)-arithmetic assumption.
q is chosen so that 10·q still fits into a computer word.
The modulus removes spurious hits.
The modulus is needed for the rolling update to be computable at all.
explanation: Keeping the numbers small is the sole motivation ✓, with the 10q word-size condition as the sizing rule ✓. The modulus *introduces* spurious hits rather than removing them ✗, and the rolling update works fine over the integers ✗.

prompt: What does automaton state st mean in FSM-based string matching, after a prefix of T has been read?
options: The last st characters read equal P[0..st−1], and no larger overlap holds.
st counts how many characters have been read in total.
st is always equal to the current shift sft.
st is the number of mismatches so far.
explanation: st is the length of the *longest* suffix of the text read so far that is also a prefix of P. Because it is recomputed from scratch at each step, it can also decrease on a mismatch — unlike a naive match counter, which would simply reset to 0.

prompt: The FSM transition function δ(st, w) — which two statements are correct?
options: δ(st, w) is the length of the longest suffix of P[0..st−1]+w that is also a prefix of P.
Reaching st = m signals a match ending at the current position, i.e. the valid shift is currentIndex − m + 1.
δ(st, w) is always st+1 or 0.
Building δ costs Θ(m), independently of the alphabet.
explanation: The longest-suffix-that-is-a-prefix rule ✓ and the match condition ✓ are the definition. δ can drop to an intermediate value between 0 and st+1, not just those two extremes ✗, and building the table needs one row per state and one column per symbol ⟹ O(m·|Σ|) ✗.

prompt: Which algorithm achieves O(n) matching time after preprocessing, with no spurious hits and no backtracking?
options: Finite-automaton matching
Naive string matching
Rabin-Karp in the worst case
None of the three guarantees O(n)
explanation: After O(m·|Σ|) preprocessing the automaton reads T in one pass with no backtracking, and its transitions are exact, so spurious hits cannot arise. Rabin-Karp's O(n+m) is only an *expected* bound; its worst case is O((n−m+1)·m), the same as naive matching.

prompt: Comparing naive, Rabin-Karp and FSM matching — which two statements are correct?
options: All three return exactly the same set of valid shifts; they differ only in preprocessing cost versus per-character matching cost.
Rabin-Karp and naive matching share the same worst case, O((n−m+1)·m).
The three algorithms use different definitions of a valid shift.
Only the FSM supports patterns over an alphabet other than letters and digits.
explanation: The preprocessing-vs-matching trade-off is exactly the axis they differ on ✓, and a pathological spurious-hit pattern degrades Rabin-Karp to the naive bound ✓. The definition of a valid shift is shared ✗, and all three work over any finite alphabet ✗.
